title: The Five Stages of Awareness
lede: Every buyer is standing on one of five rungs. Before you build an offer, you need to know which rungs your market is standing on.
deliverable: They leave with the five stages understood, and a Jarvis research report on where their market sits and what that means for the offer.
body:
This is the most useful idea in marketing, and it is sixty years old. It is not a sales trick and it is not something you use on a call. It is a way of seeing a market. Learn it here, before you write an offer, because the stage your market is on decides what your offer has to say, what your ads lead with, and how much educating you will have to do before anyone buys.

Where this comes from

Eugene Schwartz was a copywriter who wrote Breakthrough Advertising in 1966. Second hand copies sell for hundreds of dollars because the ideas in it still run most successful campaigns on the internet. His central idea is that a buyer's state of awareness decides what your message has to say first. Not your product. Not your offer. Where their head is at.

He described five stages. Each one up, the buyer knows more and needs less from you.

The five stages, properly

1. UNAWARE

They do not know they have a problem. The construction owner whose admin "handles all that" is unaware. Business feels fine. If you lead with AI, or even with the problem, you bounce straight off. The only thing that reaches an unaware buyer is a symptom they recognise in themselves: a story, a feeling, a moment they have lived. "Ever had a quote sit in the inbox for three weeks and nobody noticed?" That is a symptom. It opens the door without naming the problem yet.

2. PROBLEM AWARE

They feel the pain and can name it, but they do not know a fix exists, or they assume the fix is "hire someone" or "work harder". "We keep missing calls after five." "The office is flat out." Lead with the problem, in their words, and the cost of it. Make them feel understood and make the loss visible before any solution appears.

3. SOLUTION AWARE

They know the kind of fix exists. "AI could probably do this." "There must be a system for that." They just do not know whose, or whether it would work for them. Lead with the solution, shown, not described: a demo, a before and after, a worked case. Your product is the natural end of that story.

4. PRODUCT AWARE

They know you, or they know the options. They have seen your demo or a competitor's. They are comparing. Lead with what makes your version the right one for them specifically: the proof, the fit, the delivery, the running costs laid out honestly. Do not explain the problem again. They have moved past it and it reads as padding.

5. MOST AWARE

They want it. They just need the deal. Price, terms, start date, what happens next. Lead with the offer. Anything else is in the way.

The two mistakes that cost the most

Pitching the product to the unaware. "We build AI receptionists for trades businesses" put in front of an owner who does not think missed calls are a problem is an ad for a thing they do not want. It is not wrong, it is early.

Explaining the problem to the most aware. The owner who said "send me the proposal" and then gets three paragraphs on why missed calls cost money feels talked down to. They already climbed that rung.

Both mistakes come from the same habit: saying what you want to say instead of what they are ready to hear.

Why this matters before you write an offer

A market is not one buyer, it is a spread. Some owners in it are unaware, most are somewhere in the middle, a few are already shopping. Where the weight of the market sits changes everything about your offer.

If most of your market isYour offer has toYour marketing has to
UnawareBe built around a symptom they already feel, not the system that fixes it.Educate first. Expect a longer, more expensive path to a sale.
Problem awareName the problem in their words and put a dollar figure on it.Lead with the problem and the cost. This is the sweet spot for high ticket AI.
Solution awareShow the fix working on a business like theirs, with proof.Lead with demos and cases. Less education, more showing.
Product awareBe clearly different from what they have already seen, on fit, delivery and honesty about costs.Lead with comparison and proof. Expect competitors in the room.
Most awareBe easy to buy: clear price, clear scope, clear start.Lead with the deal. Rare in custom AI, do not plan around it.

Most high ticket AI buyers sit on rungs two and three. They feel a specific pain and have not connected it to a system, or they have heard AI can fix things and want someone to show them where. Almost nobody is most aware when they meet you, because they have never bought a custom AI system before. A market that is mostly unaware is still a market, but it is a slower and more expensive one, and you should know that before you choose it.

What Jarvis does here

You do not need to guess where your market sits. Jarvis can research it: what owners in that market are already complaining about in public, what fixes they have heard of, what they have tried, and which stage the bulk of them are on. That report is what you build the offer from.

I am considering building an AI service for this market: [describe it, for example residential builders with five to twenty staff in Australia]. Using Eugene Schwartz's five stages of awareness (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware), research where this market sits. Look at how owners in this market talk about their problems in public: forums, reviews of the software they use, job ads they post, industry groups and news. For each stage, estimate what share of the market is on it and quote or paraphrase the evidence that shows it. Then tell me: the two or three problems this market is most aware of, in their own words; the solutions they have already heard of or tried, and what they say about them; and which stage the weight of the market sits on. Finish with what that means for an offer: what the offer should lead with, how much educating will be needed before a sale, and one warning about this market if there is one. Mark every estimate as an estimate.

Do this now

Run that prompt on the market from the last lesson. Read the report and write three lines: which stage most of the market is on, the problem they are most aware of in their own words, and what your offer therefore has to lead with. If the report says the market is mostly unaware, that is not a fail, it is a cost, and it is worth knowing now rather than after you have built a demo.

Breakthrough Advertising also covers market sophistication, which is how many similar promises your market has already heard. We come back to it in Module 4 when you write ads. Awareness is the one that shapes the offer, which is why it lives here.
